procedural_history.originating_court: Judicial Commissioner for the State of Himachal Pradesh at Simla
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 26th December, 1951, of the Court of the Judicial Commissioner for the State of Himachal Pradesh at Simla in Civil Misc. Petitions Nos. 12 and 16 of 1951, rejecting two applications for the issue of writs of mandamus and certiorari under article 226 of the Constitution.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Wazir Chand made two applications under Article 226 of the Constitution to the Judicial Commissioner of Himachal Pradesh, seeking writs of mandamus to release seized medicinal herbs. The Judicial Commissioner disposed of both petitions by a single judgment, declining to grant any relief.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Wazir Chand appealed to the Supreme Court by Special Leave against the order of the Judicial Commissioner. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the order of the Judicial Commissioner, and directed an appropriate writ to issue directing the restoration to the petitioner of the goods seized by the police.

directions: set aside the order of the Judicial Commissioner
direct an appropriate writ to issue directing the restoration to the petitioner of the goods seized by the police
The appellant will have his costs of the appeals and those incurred by him in the Court of Judicial Commissioner.

issue.issue_text: Whether the determination of the legality of the seizure of goods requires a prior determination of the true title to those goods.

facts: Police from Chamba, at the instance of Jammu police, seized medicinal herbs from the actual possession of the petitioner or his servants.
The petitioner challenged the seizures as illegal and sought the return of the goods.
The lower court (Judicial Commissioner) declined to grant relief, reasoning that it was first necessary to determine the true title to the goods, which could not be done in a summary proceeding.
law: A seizure of property by the police must be sanctioned by a provision of law, such as the Code of Criminal Procedure (e.g., sections 51, 96, 98, 165).
A seizure of a citizen's property not sanctioned by law infringes the fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 19 and 31 of the Constitution of India.
Goods in the possession of a person cannot be seized except under the authority of law, even if that person may not have a lawful title to them.
application: The Supreme Court found that the petitioner's contention—that the legality of the seizure depends on legal authority, not on title—was "well founded."
The Court examined the relevant sections of the Code of Criminal Procedure and found that none of them authorized the seizure in this case.
It was noted that the police acted without a magistrate's order and that their procedure was in "utter violation of the provisions of law."

The Court explicitly rejected the idea that title must be proven first. It held that even if the petitioner was not the rightful owner, the police had no authority to deprive him of possession without a legal basis.
Because the seizure was conducted without any legal authority, it was deemed an infringement of the petitioner's fundamental rights.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the lower court's view, holding that the legality of a seizure depends on whether it was authorized by law, not on a prior determination of the true title to the goods. Since the police could not point to any legal provision authorizing their actions, the seizure from the petitioner's possession was illegal and violated his fundamental rights, regardless of who ultimately owned the goods.

issue.issue_text: Whether the seizure of goods was justified under sections 51, 96, 98, or 165 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

facts: The Chamba police, at the request of the Jammu police, seized goods from the petitioner in Chamba.
The seizure was related to an alleged offense committed in Jammu.
The seizure was conducted without a warrant or order from any magistrate in Chamba.
law: Section 51 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC) authorizes the search of arrested persons in certain circumstances.
Sections 96 and 98 of the CrPC relate to searches conducted under a magistrate's warrant.
Section 165 of the CrPC allows a police officer to conduct a search for an investigation into an offense that the officer is authorized to investigate.
application: The Court determined that none of the cited sections of the CrPC applied to the facts of the case.
Section 51 was inapplicable because no one had been arrested, no cognizable offense had been reported to the Chamba police, and no warrant had been issued by a Chamba magistrate.
Sections 96 and 98 were also inapplicable for the same reason: no warrant had been issued by a local magistrate.

Section 165 did not justify the seizure because it only applies when an officer is investigating an offense they are authorized to investigate. The Chamba police had no authority to investigate an offense that was reported to have occurred in Jammu and Kashmir.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the seizure was justified, concluding that none of the cited sections (51, 96, 98, or 165 of the CrPC) provided legal authority for the Chamba police to seize the goods. The seizure was therefore deemed to be without legal authority and in violation of the law.

issue.issue_text: Whether the petitioner is barred from seeking relief under article 226 of the Constitution because an alternative remedy under section 523 of the Criminal Procedure Code was pursued.

facts: The petitioner had previously made an application to a magistrate under section 523 of the Criminal Procedure Code to have the seized goods returned.
A revision petition filed against that dismissal was also dismissed.
law: The existence of an alternative remedy can sometimes bar a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution.
However, for this bar to apply, the alternative remedy must be a legally valid and applicable one.
application: The Court determined that section 523 of the Criminal Procedure Code had no application to the facts and circumstances of this specific case.
Consequently, the magistrate had no jurisdiction or legal authority to order the return of the goods to the petitioner under that section.
The revision application was also dismissed precisely on the grounds that the magistrate lacked jurisdiction to grant relief under section 523.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the petitioner was barred from seeking relief under Article 226. It reasoned that the supposed alternative remedy under section 523 was not a valid or effective remedy in this case, as the section was inapplicable and the magistrate had no jurisdiction to grant the relief sought.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the determination of the legality of the seizure of goods requires a prior determination of the true title to those goods.
appellant_arguments: The court below was wrong to think that determining the true title to the goods was necessary to decide the legality of the seizure.

Since the goods were seized from the actual possession of the petitioner or his servants, the only relevant question is whether the seizure was authorized by law, not whether the petitioner had a perfect title.
The petitioner should not be denied relief until he establishes his title in separate, lengthy proceedings like a civil suit.
respondent_arguments: The petitioner must first prove he has a right, title, or interest in the goods to be able to claim relief.
The question of title is a complex factual dispute involving multiple parties and allegations of forgery, which cannot be properly decided in a summary writ proceeding under Article 226.
The petitioner's proper remedy is a civil suit where evidence can be thoroughly examined, not a writ petition.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the seizure of goods was justified under sections 51, 96, 98, or 165 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
appellant_arguments: The seizure of goods was illegal and without jurisdiction.
The police action was not supported by any provision of law.
The Jammu and Kashmir police had no authority to conduct an investigation or seizure in Himachal Pradesh territory without following legal procedures, which they did not.
The seizure violated the petitioner's fundamental rights under Articles 19 and 31 of the Constitution.
respondent_arguments: The goods were related to an offense committed in Jammu, and as such, the police were entitled to seize them.
The petitioner, Wazir Chand, had no legal title to the goods.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the petitioner is barred from seeking relief under article 226 of the Constitution because an alternative remedy under section 523 of the Criminal Procedure Code was pursued.
appellant_arguments: The alternative remedy under Section 523 was not a bar because that section does not apply to the facts of this case, and the magistrate had no jurisdiction to grant relief under it.
The revision petition against the magistrate's order was also dismissed for lack of jurisdiction, proving that this was not an effective or available remedy.
respondent_arguments: The petitioner had already pursued an alternative remedy by filing an application under Section 523 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
Since the petitioner had availed another remedy, the court should not allow him to seek relief under Article 226.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A seizure of goods from a person's possession without the authority of law constitutes an infringement of their fundamental rights under Articles 19 and 31 of the Constitution. The person deprived of possession is entitled to relief under Article 226 for the restoration of the goods, and the legality of the seizure can be determined without first establishing the ultimate title to the property. The existence of an alternative remedy does not bar a writ petition if that remedy is inapplicable to the facts of the case.
obiter: It is doubtful if an offence committed in Jammu and Kashmir could be investigated by the police in India.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The seizure of goods from the petitioner's possession was entirely without legal authority, as the police action was not sanctioned by any provision of the Criminal Procedure Code or any other law. This illegal seizure constituted an infringement of the petitioner's fundamental rights under Articles 19 and 31 of the Constitution. The court's role in such a proceeding is to determine the legality of the seizure itself, not to first resolve complex disputes over title; a person cannot be deprived of property in their possession except by a procedure established by law, regardless of any underlying claims to that property.
legal_tests_applied: Whether the seizure was authorized by a provision of law, specifically sections 51, 96, 98, and 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
Whether an unauthorized seizure of goods from a person's possession constitutes an infringement of fundamental rights under Articles 19 and 31 of the Constitution.

Whether an alternative remedy under section 523 of the Criminal Procedure Code acts as a bar to a writ petition when that remedy is found to have 'no application to the facts and circumstances of this case' and the magistrate had 'no jurisdiction' to grant relief under it.
policy_considerations: The state cannot deprive a person of goods in their possession without the authority of law, even if that person's title to the goods is disputed. 'Assuming that that was so, goods in the possession of a person who is not lawfully in possession of them cannot be seized except under authority of law, and in absence of such authority, Wazir Chand could not be deprived of them.'

An illegal seizure by the state is a direct infringement of fundamental rights, warranting relief under Article 226. 'That being so, the seizure of these goods from the possession of the petitioner or his servants amounted to an infringement of his fundamental rights both under article 19 and article 31 of the Constitution and relief should have been granted to him under article 226 of the Constitution.'

A citizen should not be forced into lengthy civil proceedings to reclaim property when the initial seizure by the state was illegal and without jurisdiction; the immediate question is the legality of the state's action, not the ultimate ownership of the property.
